newsitem.title: NORWAY: NORDIC SKIING-SMIRNOV GETS LAST CHANCE TO SHINE IN 50-KM RACE.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-SMIRNOV GETS LAST CHANCE TO SHINE IN 50-KM RACE.

text.p: Vladimir Smirnov will get one last chance to shine in the Nordic skiing world championships in the grand finale, Sunday's 50-km classic cross-country race.

Smirnov, who won three golds in the last world championships, in 1995 in Thunder Bay, Canada, looks likely to be one of the heroes of a busy final weekend also featuring the women's 30-km race and the high hill ski jumping competition.
The 32-year-old from Kazakhstan is taking part in his last world championships and plans to retire after next year's Olympics in Nagano, Japan.
But he has been disappointing so far in the 10-day championships, earning his best result with a fourth place in Monday's 10-km classic.
"I wasn't expecting much from the first races," he said. "I said before it started that my main goal would be the 50-km and it still is."
Smirnov, the Olympic champion in the toughest and most prestigious of cross-country races, will have to keep an eye on Norwegian Bjorn Daehlie, almost unstoppable since the championships began.

Daehlie prefers the shorter distances and has not won a 50-km race in a major event since the 1992 Olympics in Albertville. But the form he has shown in Trondheim, where he has already won three golds, suggests it would not be wise to count him out.

"I'm really a sprinter and other guys should be stronger than me," he said after helping Norway to a brilliant victory in Friday's relay. "But it's true that I'm in great shape and if everything goes well, I might get a good result."
Daehlie said his favourite would be Russian Alexei Prokurorov, who won the opening 30-km race here and kept going strong with silver in the 10-km classic and bronze in the 15-km freestyle pursuit.
"The 50-km classic is a race I like very much and I'm confident but you shouldn't listen to Daehlie when he says he's not the favourite," said Prokurorov.
Italian Silvio Fauner, who won the 50-km world title in Thunder Bay, is far from his best and almost ruled himself out after taking bronze in the relay.
"I'm not 100 per cent fit," he said, explaining he had to leave Italy's preparation camp for the championships because his wife had just given birth to a girl.
The women's 30-km race on Saturday seems to be tailored to fit Yelena Vialbe as the Russian loves long distances.

Vialbe has won every women's race so far at the championships but she could have done without the gold for Sunday's 5-km classic, awarded to her after fellow Russian Lyubov Yegorova was stripped of her world title for testing positive for the banned stimulant Bromantan.
"I don't want to talk about it anymore," said Vialbe, who said she had been shocked and embarrassed when the news broke.

Dieter Thoma has to be the favourite for Saturday's high hill ski jumping event. The German would have won the normal hill competition had he not fallen after landing his second jump and he was the best jumper in Thursday's team event, in which Germany took bronze.
"It's good to have a medal, let's hope I can get another one," he said on Thursday.
Finn Janne Ahonen, who took gold in both the normal hill and the team competitions, also stands a chance.
Organisers, who were delighted to see some 80,000 people turn up for the relay, said they expected similar attendances at the weekend.
